Who discovered HIV? An interview with Robert Gallo and Luc Montagnier

The subject of HIV discovery has been always controversial.

Gallo did not deny that Montagnier had preceded him in isolating the virus, but he argued that it was proof of the causal relationship and the development of the blood test which were most important, and he maintained that these advances had been accomplished using a virus which had been independently isolated in his lab.

Luc Montagnier is regarded as the discoverer of HIV. He even got the Nobel Prize on 2008:

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2008 was divided, one half awarded to Harald zur Hausen "for his discovery of human papilloma viruses causing cervical cancer", the other half jointly to Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier "for their discovery of human immunodeficiency virus".

Not in most of the US. There are few states where it does apply, and many other countries, but it's generally not present in the law of countries that inherited English common law.

When this legal obligation does exist, it's called a Duty to Rescue. There are several special cases where it does apply even in most of the US. For example: parents must rescue their children, transport carriers must rescue their passengers, and property owners must rescue (some or all) people on their property. But if you're walking down the street and you see some stranger about to die, in most states, the law does not obligate you to aid them in any way nor even to call for help.

There is certainly an ethical obligation to help people in need, especially if it costs you nothing to do so (i.e., by calling 911). That is why the dude in the article is being punished. His failure to rescue was not illegal in itself, but it was morally reprehensible, and therefore the state is scrabbling for other excuses to punish him.
